newsitem.title: KENYA: Disease seen undermining Kenyan coffee production.
newsitem.headline: Disease seen undermining Kenyan coffee production.

text.p: A rise in coffee berry disease in key growing highland areas is the latest threat to Kenya's efforts to raise production, researchers said on Wednesday.

Officers at the Coffee Research Foundation (CRF) said coffee berry disease affected the crop in higland areas between July and September this year and they were preparing a full report on the extent of damage expected.
Switzerland-based coffee traders Edm. Schluter & Co Ltd said it had revised its estimates of 1996/97 production to 90,000 tonnes from a previous 100,000 tonnes owing to the disease.

But a spokesman for the Coffee Board of Kenya said it was too early to make a forecast taking into account any disease threat, although the board had already revised its own 1996/97 predictions. It first talked of 100,000 tonnes output, then revised to 96,000, and now to 95,000 tonnes.
"We do not know of any significant rise in the disease; nothing that could affect the crop that much," he said.

The Coffee Research Foundation has advocated a switch to Ruiru 11 hybrid from Kenya's traditional SL 28 and SL 32 varieties, saying Ruiru 11 was disease-resistant, had better yields and cut production costs by as much as 30 percent.
Ruiru 11 currently accounts for only five percent of production but that could be boosted by new estate interest.
Schluter said sales for the year (1995/96) totalled 111,711 tonnes, of which 28,841 was 1994/95 carryover and 82,870 tonnes of the 89,005 tonne crop was milled during 1995/96 (Oct/Sept).

"This leaves a carryover into the new coffee year of milled coffee awaiting sale of only 6,000 tonnes held by the Coffee Board of Kenya, to which should be added remaining fly-crop coffees held by private millers," Schluter said.
The coffee board has not compiled final 1995/96 figures.

"Based on our previous fly-crop (mid-crop) forecasts of 580,000 60-kg bags, we estimate only a further 170,000-180,000 bags of coffee remain to be sold between now and the arrival of the main crop," Schluter added.
It said the number of weekly export auctions in Nairobi would depend on availability of coffee still being delivered to the Coffee Board of Kenya by millers.
"With the liberalisation of the milling sector, we may also see some earlier main crop arrivals, which in the past have not appeared in auction before January," it said.

Commenting on the debate on Kenya's auction system, Schluter said "While in general the value and merits of the auction system are recognised and well appreciated, the main issue appears to be the amounts deducted from auction proceeds before funds are remitted to farmers."
"It is clear that there is continuing good support for the central auction system both in the government and in the industry in general, provided this issue can be resolved."
Coffee comes third behind tourism and tea in Kenya's foreign exchange earners. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
